Sets are filed automatically by Subject. Every folder splits into its own Topic Cards and Samplex sub-folders, sortable by Topic #. Switch the landing page to "Folders: By LE" to browse by LE instead.
This turns a clinical algorithm into its own interactive case game — instead of flashcards, you manage one patient step by step: narrative reveals, vitals/exam/labs you tap to check, then a decision with real consequences (score, feedback, a teaching pearl) before the case moves on. It's a small structured format called CASE_FORMAT (v1.0, or v1.1 for optional randomized outcomes — see below) — most easily generated by pasting your algorithm into an LLM using the prompt below, rather than hand-written. A minimal valid case looks like this: CASE_FORMAT_VERSION: 1.0 CASE_TITLE: Example START_NODE: INTRO ---------------------------------------- NODE: INTRO TYPE: SCENE NARRATIVE: A patient presents with... NEXT: DECIDE ---------------------------------------- NODE: DECIDE TYPE: DECISION QUESTION: What do you do next? CHOICE: Order the right test -> END_GOOD EXPLAIN: Correct — because... CHOICE: Skip it -> END_BAD EXPLAIN: Not ideal — because... ---------------------------------------- NODE: END_GOOD TYPE: END END_TYPE: SUCCESS SUMMARY: Nicely managed. ---------------------------------------- NODE: END_BAD TYPE: END END_TYPE: FAIL SUMMARY: That path missed something important. ---------------------------------------- SCENE nodes reveal narrative and step forward via NEXT; DECISION nodes pose a QUESTION with 2+ CHOICE lines (each can carry its own SCORE / EXPLAIN / PEARL); END nodes close the case with END_TYPE and a SUMMARY. VITALS, EXAM, LABS, IMAGING, IMAGE, and HINT are optional fields on any SCENE, DECISION, or RANDOM node, revealed on tap rather than shown all at once. Want the same case to play out differently each time — a lab result that's sometimes positive, sometimes not? Use a RANDOM node instead of SCENE: it has 2+ OUTCOME blocks (each with its own optional WEIGHT, NEXT, and narrative/findings) and the engine randomly picks one, weighted, every time that node is reached: NODE: GET_ANA TYPE: RANDOM NARRATIVE: You send the ANA titer. OUTCOME: POS WEIGHT: 1 NARRATIVE: Result: ANA positive at 1:320. NEXT: WORKUP_POSITIVE OUTCOME: NEG WEIGHT: 1 NARRATIVE: Result: ANA negative. NEXT: WORKUP_NEGATIVE The pick is locked in for that playthrough, so revisiting or resuming shows the same result — restarting the case rerolls it. See the full spec in the LLM prompt below for details.

Works with any Bluetooth gamepad — Xbox, PlayStation, 8BitDo, Switch Pro Controller, and so on. Quiz answers and menu navigation are mapped separately, so you can keep the same button for both or use different ones. Click "Remap" next to an action and press the button you want to use — then press Escape or click again to cancel.

"Directional nav" and "Shortcuts" below are optional extras, unmapped until you set them. Directional nav moves menu focus with a button press instead of a stick — handy on compact/stickless pads (like the 8BitDo Micro) that otherwise can only click whatever's already focused. Shortcuts add Back, Home, and Flag/mark-for-review to spare buttons (shoulder buttons, Minus, etc.) so nothing on the pad goes unused.

No controller detected yet — press any button on it to connect.
Bluetooth controller not showing up, but USB-C works? That's a known limitation in Chrome and other Chromium-based browsers (Edge, Brave, Opera) on macOS — they talk to Bluetooth controllers through a less reliable system path than wired ones, so this isn't something a website can fix. A few things that sometimes help:
• Fully pair the controller in System Settings → Bluetooth first (not just its own pairing button), then press a face button on it.
• Quit and reopen Chrome after pairing — a stuck Bluetooth handle sometimes needs a full relaunch, not just a page reload.
• Try Safari — its Bluetooth controller support on macOS tends to be more reliable than Chrome's.
• Otherwise, USB-C is the dependable fallback.

Works with any keyboard, wired or Bluetooth — there's nothing special to set up for a Bluetooth keyboard, it sends the exact same key presses as a wired one. By default, quiz answers can be picked with 1-4, A-D, or U/I/O/P, and Enter or Space moves to the next card. Set a personal shortcut below for any action and it works alongside those defaults rather than replacing them. Click "Remap", then press the key you want to use — Escape or clicking again cancels.

The app quietly tracks response time, answer confidence, and which wrong answers you pick, all stored locally on this device only — never sent anywhere. It uses this to estimate mastery per card, schedule reviews, and spot recurring mix-ups, and to power the "Cards to review" and study-priority features on the Stats screen.

A quick optional 1–5 tap after you answer. Skipping it is always fine — it just makes the mastery estimate a bit more precise.

Recomputes mastery/review scheduling from your full answer history. Useful after importing a backup, or if something looks out of sync — normal use never requires this.

Your study data and your background are backed up separately. Importing a study backup will never change your current background.
Use the background backup only when you actually want to move or restore your wallpaper, video, palette, and blur settings.
Export just the sets themselves — none of your stats, streaks, session history, or "completed" marks come along. The other person imports it with the same "Import study data" button above, and it's added as new sets without touching anything already on their device.
On iPhone/iPad, storage for a page can behave differently depending on how it was opened (Safari directly vs. a Files app preview, a Home Screen icon, another app's built-in browser, or Private Browsing) — check here if a backup import doesn't seem to stick.
If a fix doesn't seem to take effect after you've updated the file on GitHub, check the version below — if it looks old, tap Force refresh to bypass any cached copy.
